title: Cap. II Arg. 7: Apoc. 3:11 — hold fast / crown grounds foresight-perseverance
latin: Ultimum testimonium petitur ex Apoc. iii. 11. Tene quod habes, ne alius accipiat coronam tuam. Ex hisce verbis patet coronam gloriae amitti posse vita impia: Deus ergo neminem praedestinat ad hanc coronam gloriae, nisi quia videt illum ad extremum in pietate & fide perseveraturum. Si enim absque hac praevisione quenquam praedestinaret, incerta redderetur praedestinatio, & posset per suam infirmitatem aut pravitatem a gloria excidere, quem Deus voluit ad gloriam praedestinare.
pass_a: The last testimony is taken from Revelation 3:11: Hold what you have, lest another take your crown. From these words it is plain that the crown of glory can be lost by an impious life: God therefore predestines no one to this crown of glory except because he sees that that person will persevere to the end in piety and faith. For if he predestined anyone without this foresight, predestination would be rendered uncertain, and the one whom God willed to predestine to glory could fall from glory through his own weakness or wickedness.
pass_b: Last: they take Revelation 3:11 — "Hold what you have, lest another take your crown." From that they say the crown of glory can be lost by an ungodly life, so God predestines no one to that crown unless he sees the person will persevere to the end in piety and faith. Without that foresight, they argue, predestination would be unsure — someone God meant for glory could drop out by weakness or wickedness.

lemmas.gloss: foresight of final perseverance as condition

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7: crown of ministry vs heavenly glory — alternate reading first
latin: Respondeo, haec verba non minore probabilitate ad coronam ministerii accommodari posse quam ad coronam caelestis gloriae, hoc nimirum sensu; Tene quod habes, id est, Episcopale officium constanter & diligenter exerce: ne alius accipiat coronam tuam, hoc est, ne, si tu negligentem te ostenderis, alius, te rejecto, in locum tuum sufficiatur. Sed quia eadem verba possunt haud incommode, & solent a multis, ad coronam caelestis gloriae referri, hoc sensu admisso, respondemus.
pass_a: I answer: these words can with no less probability be fitted to the crown of ministry than to the crown of heavenly glory, in this sense: Hold what you have — that is, exercise the episcopal office constantly and diligently; lest another take your crown — that is, lest, if you show yourself negligent, another, you being rejected, be put in your place. But because the same words can not inconveniently, and are accustomed by many to be referred to the crown of heavenly glory, that sense being admitted, we reply.
pass_b: Reply: the words fit the crown of ministry at least as well as heavenly glory — "Hold what you have" as keep the bishop's office steadily and carefully; "lest another take your crown" as lest, if you prove negligent, someone else is put in your place after you are set aside. Still, many read them of the heavenly crown without strain. Take that sense, and we answer as follows.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7 Primo: elect cannot lose crown — certainty from causal chain, not bare foresight
latin: Primo, Non posse praedestinatos amittere coronam gloriae: hanc tamen certitudinem adipiscendi coronam non oriri ex necessitate cogente illos ad vitam aeternam, neque niti mera Dei praescientia intuente quid illi ex libero suo arbitrio facturi sint; sed fundatam esse in illo causarum ordine quem specialis quaedam Divina providentia ad salutem electorum infallibiliter producendam concatenavit. Hanc certitudinem, non nudae praescientiae, sed causalitatis Apostolus indicavit Rom. viii. ubi docet ita Deum instituisse & gubernare ordinem causarum ad promovendam salutem electorum, ut omnia etiam illa quae saluti illorum infesta videntur, tamen cooperentur illis in aeternum bonum animarum; versu 28. & seq. usque ad finem capitis.
pass_a: First: the predestined cannot lose the crown of glory; yet this certainty of obtaining the crown does not arise from a necessity that forces them to eternal life, nor does it rest on bare divine foreknowledge looking at what they will do from their free will; but it is founded in that order of causes which a certain special Divine providence has chained together for infallibly producing the salvation of the elect. This certainty — not of bare foresight, but of causality — the Apostle indicated in Romans 8, where he teaches that God has so instituted and governs the order of causes for advancing the elect's salvation that even those things which seem hostile to their salvation nevertheless work together for them unto the eternal good of their souls; verse 28 and following to the end of the chapter.
pass_b: First: the predestined cannot lose the crown of glory. That certainty does not come from a force that drags them into eternal life, nor from bare foresight of what free will will do. It rests on the chain of causes special providence has linked so the elect's salvation is produced without fail. Paul marks that as causality, not naked foresight — Romans 8: God so set and steers the order of causes for the elect that even what looks hostile still works for their souls' eternal good (vv. 28ff to the chapter's end).

lemmas.gloss: all things work for elect's good

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7: Augustine — if an elect perished God would be deceived and overcome
latin: Atque hinc est quod Augustinus infert, si aliquis electorum a Deo discederet mutabilitate liberi sui arbitrii, quod non modo falleretur Deus, sed vinceretur, quia scilicet non modo praevidit electos fore glorificandos, sed invicta causarum concatenatione hoc efficere decrevit. Horum (id est, electorum) si quisquam perit, fallitur Deus; sed nemo eorum perit, quia non fallitur Deus: horum si quisquam perit vitio humano, vincitur Deus; sed nemo eorum perit, quia nulla re vincitur Deus, De corrept. & grat. cap. 7. Cur Deus vinceretur si electus periret vitio propriae voluntatis? Quia scilicet in se Deus suscepit, ut omnibus electis non nudam & languidam possibilitatem, sed firmam, certam & invictam perseverandi voluntatem ingeneraret.
pass_a: And hence Augustine infers that if any of the elect departed from God by the mutability of his free will, God would not only be deceived but overcome — because he not only foresaw that the elect would be glorified, but decreed to effect this by an invincible chain of causes. Of these (that is, the elect), if anyone perishes, God is deceived; but none of them perishes, because God is not deceived: of these, if anyone perishes by human fault, God is overcome; but none of them perishes, because God is overcome by nothing (On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 7). Why would God be overcome if an elect perished by the fault of his own will? Because God took it on himself to generate in all the elect not a bare and languid possibility, but a firm, certain, and invincible will to persevere.
pass_b: That is why Augustine says: if any elect left God by free will's changeableness, God would not only be deceived but beaten — he not only foresaw their glorification; he decreed to bring it about by an unbeatable chain of causes. On Rebuke and Grace 7: if any of them perishes, God is deceived — but none does, for God is not deceived; if any perishes by human fault, God is overcome — but none does, for nothing overcomes God. Why "overcome" if an elect fell by his own will's fault? Because God undertook to plant in every elect not a thin bare possibility, but a firm, sure, unconquered will to persevere.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7: weak will can lose; under divine direction the elect cannot
latin: Quamvis igitur, si spectentur electi ex propriae voluntatis infirmitate, possunt amittere coronam; tamen si spectentur, qua subjacet haec illorum voluntas efficacissimae directioni Divinae, non possunt illam amittere.
pass_a: Although therefore, if the elect are viewed from the weakness of their own will, they can lose the crown; yet if they are viewed insofar as this their will lies under the most efficacious Divine direction, they cannot lose it.
pass_b: So if you look only at the elect's weak will, they can lose the crown. Look at that same will under God's most effective direction, and they cannot.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7 Secundo: foresight of perseverance concurrent — not prior cause of predestination
latin: Secundo, quod dicunt adversarii, Deum neminem praedestinare ad coronam nisi quem praevidet perseveraturum, eatenus pro vero admittendum, quatenus ponit easdem singulares personas quae praedestinantur ad gloriam, esse praevisas simul a Deo ut perseveraturas in gratia. Sed quatenus supponit hanc praevisionem esse causam praedestinationis, & secundum nostrum modum intelligendi illa priorem, est omnino repudiandum.
pass_a: Second: what the adversaries say — that God predestines no one to the crown except whom he foresees will persevere — is to be admitted as true insofar as it posits that the same singular persons who are predestined to glory are at the same time foreseen by God as going to persevere in grace. But insofar as it supposes this foresight to be the cause of predestination, and prior to it according to our way of understanding, it is altogether to be rejected.
pass_b: Second: when opponents say God predestines to the crown only those he foresees will persevere, grant it this far — the same people predestined to glory are also foreseen as going to persevere in grace. Reject it when they make that foresight the cause of predestination, and prior to it in our order of thought.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 7 close: hortations keep elect persevering — scripture proofs of foresight-election end
latin: Postremo, quod attinet ad ipsorum verborum formulam, recte Augustinus, De corrept. & grat. cap. 13. Perseveraturis sanctis sic ista dicuntur, quasi eos perseveraturos habeatur incertum: non aliter enim hoc audire debent, quibus expedit non altum sapere, sed timere. Hujusmodi ergo hortationes ipsis electis adhibentur, non quod incerta sit illorum praedestinatio, aut ex mutabilitate arbitrii illorum pendula, sed quod hoc medio hortationum, aliisque quae Deus apta esse novit, efficiat ut in gratia & sanctitate perseverent. Atque haec praecipua testimonia Scripturarum sunt, quae ad probandam electionem ex praevisione meritorum afferuntur. Si quae alia occurrant, ex hisce quae explicata sunt veram illorum sententiam desumere in promptu erit. A testimoniis ergo ad rationes adversariorum veniamus.
pass_a: Last: as for the formula of the words themselves, Augustine rightly says (On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 13) that these things are said to the saints who will persevere as if it were held uncertain that they will persevere: for they ought not to hear it otherwise, for whom it is expedient not to be high-minded but to fear. Such exhortations are therefore applied to the elect themselves, not because their predestination is uncertain or hangs on the mutability of their will, but because by this means of exhortations, and by others which God knows to be apt, he brings it about that they persevere in grace and holiness. And these are the chief testimonies of the Scriptures which are brought to prove election from foresight of merits. If any others occur, it will be ready to take their true sense from these which have been explained. From testimonies, therefore, let us come to the adversaries' reasons.
pass_b: Last, on the wording itself: Augustine (On Rebuke and Grace 13) says these lines are spoken to saints who will persevere as if their perseverance were unsure — they need to hear it that way, not to be proud but to fear. So the elect get such warnings not because their predestination is shaky or hangs on free will's change, but because by exhortation and other means God knows fit, he makes them persevere in grace and holiness. Those are the main Scripture proofs used for election from foresight of merits. Any further texts take their sense from these. From the texts, then, to the adversaries' reasons.
